source: Swanson (1990) Influence of metacognitive knowledge and aptitude on problem solving, J Educ Psych 82:306-314
finding: 2 x 2 design crossing high/low aptitude with high/low metacognitive knowledge in children. High-metacognition children solved problems better than low-metacognition children at both aptitude levels. This is the source of the claim that metacognition compensates for low IQ.
numbers: Exact N, grades and effect sizes NOT verified (only abstract-level summaries seen; publisher pages blocked).
limits: Design forced IQ and metacognition to be orthogonal (per a later critique), so it cannot show how independent they are in real populations. No direct replication found in search. Measure was a questionnaire (offline).
agent_relevance: The compensation claim rests on one questionnaire study of children. Weak support for S6, not a measured effect size.

source: Muncer et al. (2021) Meta-analysis: metacognition and math performance in adolescence, Educ Psych Rev
finding: Metacognition correlates positively with math performance in 11-16 year olds, and the link is stronger when metacognition is measured online during the task.
numbers: 74 effect sizes, 29 studies, 30 populations: r = .37, 95% CI [.29,.44]. Online measures r = .54 (k=14, I2 79%) vs offline r = .30 (k=60, I2 99.9%), p=.034. Measured during a math task r = .48 vs not during r = .28 (p=.027).
quote: significant positive correlation between metacognition and math performance in adolescence
limits: Correlational. Heterogeneity extremely high (I2 up to 99.96%). Online measures are few (k=14). Cannot say metacognition causes performance.
agent_relevance: Signals read from behaviour during the task predict success better than self-report. Supports code-measured progress signals over model self-assessment.

source: Muncer et al. (2021), summary of earlier meta-analyses (Ohtani & Hisasaka 2018; Dent & Koenka)
finding: Earlier meta-analyses found the same online/offline split in general academic performance.
numbers: Ohtani & Hisasaka 2018 as cited: online measures r = .53 (90% CI .45-.61), offline r = .23 (.20-.26). Dent & Koenka: r = .20 (95% CI .16-.24) over 61 studies.
limits: Secondary citation inside Muncer; original Ohtani paper not opened. Offline questionnaires dominate the literature and dilute the average.
agent_relevance: Most human 'metacognition helps' evidence is questionnaire-based and weak (r about .2). Do not import it as strong.

source: Ten-meta-analyses summary page (globalmetacognition.com)
finding: Secondary table of ten meta-analyses of metacognition instruction and ability. Instruction effects run roughly g = 0.3 to 1.0.
numbers: Dignath & Buttner 2008: 74 studies, 357 effects, mean 0.69. de Boer 2018: 48 interventions, g=.50 post, .63 follow-up. Theobald 2021: 49 studies, g=.37. Eberhart et al: g=.48 immediate, .29 longer-term. Higgins 2005: .62 (.96 for metacognitive interventions). Dent & Koenka 2015: r=.20. Muncer 2021: r=.37.
limits: Blog-level secondary summary. Metrics differ (g, d, r) and are not comparable. Some entries (Sercenia & Prudente g=1.6) look inflated. Verify against primary papers.
agent_relevance: Realistic size of a regulation intervention for humans is moderate (g about .4 to .7), not large.

source: Dignath & Buttner (2008) Components of fostering self-regulated learning, Metacognition and Learning
finding: Meta-analysis of self-regulation training at primary (49 studies) and secondary (35 studies) level. Training works at both levels.
numbers: 357 effect sizes; mean 0.69 (from secondary summary). Larger when researchers delivered training than regular teachers. Larger in math than reading/writing. Metacognitive reflection stronger in secondary school.
limits: Full text not opened (paywall). Numbers from search summaries. Researcher-delivered advantage suggests an implementation or developer-bias moderator.
agent_relevance: Effects shrink when delivered by non-developers. Expect the same for a scaffold tuned by its authors on their own tasks.

source: Donker et al. (2014) Effectiveness of learning strategy instruction on academic performance, Educ Res Review 11:1-26
finding: Strategy instruction improves academic performance. Best strategies differ by domain. Metacognitive-knowledge instruction helps in every domain.
numbers: 58 studies, 95 interventions, 180 effect sizes. Hedges g: writing 1.25, science 0.73, mathematics 0.66, comprehension reading 0.36.
limits: Abstract-level numbers via a library record; full text blocked (403).
agent_relevance: Which regulation step helps depends on domain. Supports learning conditional knowledge per task class.

source: de Boer, Donker, Kostons, van der Werf (2018) Long-term effects of metacognitive strategy instruction, Educ Res Review 24:98-115
finding: Metacognitive strategy instruction effect did not fade at follow-up. It rose slightly.
numbers: 48 interventions. Hedges g = 0.50 at posttest, 0.63 at follow-up. Low-SES students gained most long-term. Interventions including rehearsal had lower long-term effects. Other specific strategy types did not moderate.
limits: Full text not opened (hosts blocked). Follow-up samples are a subset and may be self-selected.
agent_relevance: Taught regulation can persist in humans because people internalise it. A frozen model cannot, so persistence does not transfer.

source: Veenman and colleagues: mixed model of intelligence and metacognition (Veenman & Elshout 1991; Veenman, Kok & Blote 2005; Prins et al. 2006)
finding: Rival accounts: intelligence model, independency model, mixed model. The mixed model (metacognitive skill overlaps with ability but adds prediction beyond it) is best supported. Metacognition matters most at the boundary of what the learner knows.
numbers: No numbers verified. Reported qualitatively: metacognitive skillfulness, not intellectual ability, is essential when learners work at the boundary of their knowledge.
limits: Known only from search summaries. The mixed model partly contradicts Swanson's independence framing.
agent_relevance: Suggests S6 review should fire at the knowledge boundary (impasse), not each step. Matches G1.

source: Small studies of metacognitive prompts 2021-2025 (Engelmann et al. 2021; Klar et al. 2024; others)
finding: Several small randomised studies of metacognitive prompts found no benefit.
numbers: Engelmann 2021: 28 prompted vs 29 control, no clear effect. Klar 2024: 51 prompted vs 150 controls, no benefit, half did not use prompts as intended. Higher-education lab study 2025: N=110, prompts not a significant predictor. Qatar K-12 math: N=113, no difference.
limits: Snippet-level only. Small samples, low power. A null is not a zero effect. Prompt uptake was poor.
agent_relevance: Telling a learner to monitor is not monitoring. A scaffold that forces the step in code avoids the uptake problem.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without oracle labels, asking the model to review and fix its own answer does not help and often hurts on reasoning tasks. Earlier gains came from oracle labels deciding when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 after 1, 3, 5 calls. GSM8K 75.9, 75.1, 74.7. CommonSenseQA 75.8, 38.1, 41.8. HotpotQA 26.0, 25.0, 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0; CSQA 82.0, 79.5, 80.0; HotpotQA 49, 49, 43. With oracle labels GPT-4 HotpotQA reached 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Few benchmarks, 2023 models, HotpotQA n=100. Not a test of 2025 reasoning models. Prompts were generic 'review your answer'.
agent_relevance: Direct hit on the 'Is it getting me anywhere?' self-question: with no external signal it fails. S6 must be triggered by a code check (G1, G2).

source: Huang et al. (2024) control: multi-agent debate and self-consistency at equal compute
finding: Equal-compute comparison: multi-agent debate does no better than plain self-consistency.
numbers: GSM8K GPT-3.5: standard 76.7; self-consistency 82.5 (3 responses), 85.3 (6), 88.2 (9); debate about 83 at 3 and 6 responses (table text garbled). Style-type task (CommonGen-Hard): self-correct 53.0 vs plain 44.0 (improves).
limits: Extracted table is garbled; exact debate rows uncertain. Style tasks differ from reasoning.
agent_relevance: Compare any regulation step with a same-compute sampling baseline. Extra calls alone give gains.

source: Tyen et al. (2024, ACL Findings) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Splits self-correction into finding the mistake and fixing it. Finding is the bottleneck. Fixing is robust once the step is known.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 5 tasks, traces 15% correct and 85% incorrect. Best direct step-level mistake finding (GPT-4) about 52.9% overall. Backtracking with true mistake location: wrong traces gained +18 to +44 points per task (multistep arithmetic +43.9, Dyck +36.9, tracking +23.5) while right traces lost 0 to 11. Random location: wrong traces +5 to +21 but right traces -7 to -16. A small classifier trained out-of-domain beat prompting a large model at location.
quote: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
limits: Mistake location is oracle in the main test. Traces from PaLM 2, tasks synthetic.
agent_relevance: Supports 'code locates, model fixes' (G2). Monitoring must be an external detector. Correction can stay with the model.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024, TACL) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey
finding: No prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from the same prompted LLM on general tasks. It works with reliable external feedback, after large-scale fine-tuning, or on tasks exceptionally suited to it.
numbers: Qualitative: (1) no success with prompted-LLM feedback outside suited tasks, (2) good with external tools (code interpreter, search), (3) fine-tuning enables it. Gives a checklist for fair evaluation.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Read abstract, intro and framework only; not every cited result checked. Covers papers to May 2024.
agent_relevance: Confirms the design: regulation by external tests, not self-talk. The checklist applies to benchmarking our S6.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) SCoRe: training language models to self-correct via reinforcement learning
finding: Multi-turn RL on self-generated data makes second-try correction positive. The base model gets worse on a second try.
numbers: MATH500, Gemini 1.5 Flash. Base: 52.6% then 41.4% (-11.2; right-to-wrong 15.8%, wrong-to-right 4.6%). Self-Refine 52.8 then 51.8. STaR 53.6 then 54.0. Pair-SFT 52.4 then 54.2. SCoRe 60.0 then 64.4 (+4.4). Abstract: self-correction improved 15.6% on MATH and 9.1% on HumanEval.
quote: self-correction capability has been shown to be severely lacking in current LLMs
limits: Needs training (we do not train). Part of the gain is a better first attempt (52.6 to 60.0). Gemini only.
agent_relevance: Self-correction can be taught but not by prompting. An untrained loop needs external checks. A bare second pass cost the base model 11.2 points.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: language agents with verbal reinforcement learning
finding: Agents write a verbal reflection after a failed trial and retry. Large gains when the failure signal is real (environment reward, unit tests).
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs GPT-4 80%. ALFWorld: ReAct+Reflexion completed 130 of 134 tasks. Authors report +22% ALFWorld, +20% HotPotQA, +11% HumanEval over baselines. Paper notes self-written tests can pass a wrong solution (false positive).
limits: Huang et al. show some of these gains rely on oracle correctness labels for stopping. Internal test suites can be wrong.
agent_relevance: Reflection after a real failure signal works. Reference for a G2-compliant S6. Guard against false-positive passes (G3).

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? MAST
finding: 1,600+ annotated traces across 7 frameworks. Many failures are monitoring and verification failures.
numbers: Annotator kappa 0.88. Category shares: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%. Step repetition 15.7%, not recognising task completion 12.4%, reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%, incorrect verification 9.1%, no or incomplete verification 8.2%, premature termination 6.2%. One role-spec and verification intervention gave +9.4% task success.
quote: verifiers perform only superficial checks, despite being prompted to perform thorough verification
limits: Failures labelled by an LLM judge (kappa 0.77 with humans). 2024 frameworks and models. Interventions tested on two systems.
agent_relevance: Real agents loop and fail to stop. These are direct targets for a code-run progress and stop detector.

source: Self-Correction Bench (COLM 2026): the self-correction blind spot
finding: Models fix an error attributed to the user but not the identical error attributed to themselves.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%. Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. Non-math domains 62.8%. Of models' own natural errors only 4.3% to 10.8% were caught when shown externally. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces cut the blind spot 76.0%. Appending 'Wait' cut it 89.3% with no training. External errors drew 179.5% more correction markers on GSM8K-SC.
limits: Constructed error injection. Mostly non-reasoning models. Prefill needed, so few closed models tested.
agent_relevance: A one-word trigger can switch on correction; the scaffold can add it only after a failed check (G1). Present the output without authorship (G5).

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: suppress stopping and append 'Wait' so the model keeps checking. Accuracy rises with extra thinking.
numbers: s1-32B on AIME24 rose from 50% to 57% with budget forcing; trained on 1,000 samples.
limits: Trained model. Gains flatten. Forced waiting can lengthen output without raising accuracy on easy items. | NOTE (cross-check): AIME24 50.0 -> 56.7 (s1 Table 1) confirmed.
agent_relevance: Forced extra review on a schedule is the opposite of G1. Use a signal to decide when.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? Overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models spend far too many tokens on easy items; extra solutions add no accuracy.
numbers: Self-training cut token output 48.6% while maintaining accuracy on MATH500 with QwQ-32B-Preview. One variant cut tokens 22.3%.
quote: reduce token output by 48.6% while maintaining accuracy
limits: One model family; MATH500 is mostly easy. Metrics defined by the authors.
agent_relevance: Supports the cost half of S6: a stop rule saves compute. Regulation includes stopping, not only more checking.

source: Wang & Zhao (2023) Metacognitive prompting improves understanding in large language models
finding: A five-stage prompt (understand, judge, evaluate, decide, confidence) is reported to beat chain-of-thought on language-understanding tasks.
numbers: Numbers not recorded (local file was removed by another process before extraction).
limits: Prompt only. Language-understanding tasks, not multi-step reasoning. Likely subject to Huang's critique of self-judgment.
agent_relevance: Use as a prompted-regulation arm to test, not as evidence.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve prompting
finding: Asking for a plan first, then execution, beats 'think step by step' on arithmetic with GPT-3 (text-davinci-003).
numbers: Zero-shot-CoT: MultiArith 83.8, GSM8K 56.4, AddSub 85.3, AQuA 38.9, SingleEq 88.1, SVAMP 69.9, average 70.4. PS+: GSM8K 59.3, AQuA 46.0, SVAMP 75.7, average 76.7. Error analysis of 46 wrong GSM8K answers: calculation 7%, missing step 12%, semantic misunderstanding 27%.
limits: Older model, arithmetic only. Gains on stronger reasoners not measured here.
agent_relevance: The planning step gives a small but measurable gain: +2.9 on GSM8K, +6.3 on the average.

source: Didolkar et al. (2024) Metacognitive capabilities of LLMs: an exploration in mathematical problem solving
finding: The model labels math questions by skill; routing exemplars by skill label improves accuracy. This is conditional knowledge: which method fits which problem.
numbers: MATH: +11.6% over chain-of-thought, +3.5% over complex CoT and topic-based. Code solutions: +7.52% over PAL. About +4.0% over CoT with self-consistency.
limits: Labels assigned by GPT-4. Gain may come from exemplar retrieval rather than metacognition. No human comparison.
agent_relevance: Conditional knowledge (which operator fits which class) is learnable and helps. Fits the class-record idea.

source: Inference across reviewed meta-analyses: does regulation compensate for low ability?
finding: The meta-analyses show metacognition-performance links and low-SES gains, but none confirms the strict compensation claim at effect-size level.
numbers: de Boer 2018: low-SES gained most at follow-up (qualitative). Muncer 2021: moderators were measure type and task complexity, not learner ability. Theobald 2021 (secondary): lower prior performers gained more in resource management only.
limits: Inference across sources, not one test. Swanson's numbers unseen.
agent_relevance: Compensation by regulation is plausible but unproven in effect-size terms. Do not base the scaffold on it.

source: Cross-source pattern in LLM regulation studies (Huang, Tyen, Kamoi, Kumar, Shinn)
finding: Intrinsic review fails; locating by an external signal and then correcting works; fine-tuning teaches it.
numbers: Intrinsic review lost 1 to 12 points on GSM8K for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 over 2 to 3 extra rounds; oracle location gave +18 to +44 on wrong traces; SCoRe +4.4 net over two turns; Reflexion 91% on HumanEval.
limits: Different models, tasks and years. Not a pooled estimate.
agent_relevance: The consistent moderator is the source of the error signal, not the wording of the self-question.

source: Moderator summary for our agent: measure, task complexity, delivery, domain
finding: Human moderators: online vs offline measure (r .54 vs .30), task complexity (larger for complex), delivery (researchers larger than teachers), domain (writing 1.25 vs reading 0.36).
numbers: Muncer 2021 numbers opened; Donker and Dignath numbers from summaries only.
limits: Cross-study moderators are confounded (domain with age with measure).
agent_relevance: Test the scaffold on complex multi-step tasks and expect smaller effects on easy ones.
